info.title: Firetower
info.description: The Firetower control plane: API, scheduling, and worker transports.

post.summary: Re-ask every reachable host what it has.
post.description:
Hosts we can't reach are skipped rather than failing the request: their last
answer stays on screen, which is more useful than an error.

delete.summary: Forget an agent's configuration and any credential with it.

post.summary: Sign an agent in with a device code, on a host.
post.description:
Returns as soon as there is a code to show. Approving it happens in a
browser, wherever the person is, and can take a quarter of an hour — so the
waiting is a task here rather than a request left open.

Only Codex works this way. Claude Code hands you a token to paste, which is
`configure_agent`.

200.description: Changed. Every other browser is signed out.

400.description: Too short, or the current one is wrong

get.summary:
Replay. The live feed is the event stream; this is the backfill after a hard
refresh, and the fallback when a stream can't be held open.

get.description:
Server-sent events rather than a socket: the data only ever flows down, and
the browser then supplies reconnection and replay for free. Each event
carries its sequence number as the SSE id, so a client that drops picks up
exactly where it left off via `Last-Event-ID` — the resume cursor is the
platform's problem, not ours.

post.summary: Add somewhere for agents to run.
post.description:
Connecting happens straight away rather than on the next restart, so a
mistake in an address is a message here instead of a host that silently
never works.

A host that doesn't answer is still created, and comes back `Unreachable`
with a `diagnosis` saying why and what to run. That is not the same as the
request failing: what someone typed was accepted, and the machine at the
other end has something to fix. Only what we can rule out from here —
an empty address, a key that isn't a key, a name already taken — is a 400.

post.summary: Try a machine without adding it.
post.description:
Adding used to create the row and then connect, which left a host behind
whenever the first attempt failed — and with Firetower's own key, the first
attempt failing is the ordinary path rather than the exception: a machine has
not been told about the key yet.

So the interface asks this first. Nothing is stored, so a mistyped address
leaves nothing to delete, and retrying is a button rather than a form to fill
in again.

delete.summary: Forget a host, and take its container with it.
delete.description:
Refuses while sessions are running unless `force`, in which case they are
told to end first — an agent that gets to shut down leaves its worktree and
tmux session behind cleanly, rather than having the floor pulled out.

A container Firetower started is Firetower's to stop. One it merely found
running is not, and start-up says as much when it adopts nothing.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: End running sessions instead of refusing

patch.description:
The name and nothing else: what a host *is* was settled when it was added,
and pointing it somewhere different is removing it and adding another.

post.summary: Try a host again now, instead of waiting out the backoff.
post.description:
The supervisor would get there on its own; this is for the moment just after
you have fixed the machine and would rather not wait.

post.summary: Stop sending work here, or start again.

delete.summary: Sign out: forget the token and stop any authorization still waiting.

post.summary: Start an authorization and begin waiting for it to be approved.
post.description:
Returns immediately with the code to show. The waiting happens here rather
than in the browser so that closing the tab doesn't abandon it.

post.summary: Register an application to authorize against.
post.description:
Asked twice on purpose: once in the setup wizard, where it is skippable,
and again on the connect-a-repository screen at the moment somebody wants
the thing it enables. Stored rather than configured, so it takes effect
without a restart.

get.summary: Who this person's commits are authored as on this host.

put.summary: Say who your commits should be authored as.
put.description:
Kept as `set`, which the derived answer never overwrites: the reason to
type one is that what the host said was not the address you wanted on your
branches.

delete.summary: Go back to whatever the git host says you are called.

get.summary: What the authorized account can see. This is the picker's data.

post.summary: Can we reach it, and what is it called?
post.description:
Answered by a worker, because the worker is what holds the credentials and
what will do the clone. Anything decided here would be a guess about someone
else's network.

delete.description:
Refuses while sessions are still running on it — silently orphaning live
work is worse than making someone finish or stop it first. The on-disk
mirror is a cache and stays; it is not this button's business.

get.summary: The branches a session can start from.
get.description:
Asked of the remote rather than read from a cached list: a branch pushed a
minute ago should be offerable, and the probe that answers this is the same
one that validated the repository in the first place.

get.summary: The variables a session on this repository will be given.
get.description:
Names, never values. One value comes back from one route, the same one
everything else in the vault uses, and that route writes to the log first.

get.summary: What is stored, and every time it was touched.
get.description:
Names and history only. A value comes back from exactly one route, which is
`reveal_secret` below, and that one writes to the log before it answers.

put.summary: Replace a credential with a new one.
put.description:
Only for a name that already exists. Storing under an arbitrary name would
let this screen fill up with values nothing ever reads — what a credential is
*for* is decided where it is used, not here.

delete.description:
Whatever used it goes back to having none — an agent shows as needing one
again, a git host shows as not authorized. The log entry stays.

post.summary: Put a credential on screen.
post.description:
A `POST` because it changes something: it writes a `Reveal` into the access
log, which is what makes this defensible at all. A `GET` would also sit in
browser history and proxy logs, which a credential shouldn't.

This is the one route that hands a stored value back, and it exists because
a credential you cannot inspect is one you cannot verify or copy elsewhere.
The cost is real: anything that can reach this API can read every token
here, and the log is what is left to notice it.

get.description:
Without `limit` this returns everything, which is what the dashboard wants —
it has to see every running session to say anything true about the fleet.
With one, it pages.

post.summary: End every session that is still running.
post.description:
Destructive in the same way as ending one, multiplied — every workspace goes
and anything unpushed with it. The count comes back so the interface can say
what it did rather than guess.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Remove it here even though its host isn't answering

patch.description:
The name only. A session's number is what other things point at, so it is
fixed for as long as the session exists — renaming is for the half a person
reads.

post.summary: Answer something the agent is waiting on.
post.description:
Until this arrives the agent is stopped, holding the tool call open. There
is no timeout anywhere on that path: somebody may be asleep, and an agent
that gave up and denied would be worse than one that waited.

post.summary: Put a file into the session's workspace.
post.description:
For everything that is not a picture. A picture goes inside the message,
because the model looks at it; anything else is better as a file the agent
can read, grep, unzip or edit with the tools it already has — and it costs
nothing until it does, so a large archive never has to fit in a prompt.

post.summary: Commit the work, or the part of it somebody kept.
post.description:
Everything by default, because that is what an unattended session wants.
Naming files is for the review sheet, where somebody has just looked at each
one and unticked the lockfile.

get.summary: Everything the agent has said so far.
get.description:
A snapshot. Use the stream for a session that is still running — this is for
one that has finished, and for a first paint that wants to be a single
request rather than a connection.

Server-sent events, like the session feed: it only ever flows down, and the
browser supplies reconnection for free. Each event carries its line number
as the SSE id, so a client that drops resumes from `Last-Event-ID` and the
cursor is the platform's problem rather than ours.

post.summary: What the agent would call this work.
post.description:
Runs on the host, where the code is — a short-lived agent reading the diff,
not a turn in the session. A hidden turn is still a turn: it would land in
the transcript, spend the session's tokens and move its context meter, and a
session somebody is about to carry on working in should not be closer to
full because something wanted a sentence for a form.

get.summary: What this session changed, file by file.
get.description:
Split on the server: it is a pure function over text that is easy to get
subtly wrong, and doing it once here beats doing it in every client.

parameters.name: checkout
parameters.description: Which checkout, by its path in the workspace. Every one when omitted.

get.summary: A file out of the workspace, streamed.
get.description:
Chunked all the way through: the worker reads it in pieces, the pieces cross
one pipe shared with every terminal on that machine, and they go straight
out to the browser rather than being collected here first.

get.summary: What is in a directory of a session's workspace.
get.description:
Paths are relative to the workspace and stay there: the worker refuses
anything with a `..` in it, and describes a symbolic link rather than
following it.

post.summary: Stop what the agent is doing, without ending the session.

get.description:
A websocket rather than the event stream: this is the one thing in Firetower
that genuinely flows both ways, byte at a time, and where latency is felt.

Output arrives as binary frames of raw terminal bytes. Input goes back the
same way; a text frame is a control message, which today means resizing.

parameters.name: shell
parameters.description: A shell of your own rather than the agent's terminal

post.summary: Open a pull request for this session's branch.
post.description:
An API call to the git host rather than a git operation, so it happens here
with the token we already hold — the same shape as listing repositories.

post.summary: Push every branch, so the work outlives the workspace.
post.description:
Each repository is pushed to its own remote. One that has nothing new is
skipped rather than refused: it is a repository this change did not touch.

post.summary: Check another repository into a session that is already running.
post.description:
The same work as bring-up, done once more. The agent is told afterwards,
because an agent that is not told has no reason to look.

post.summary: Stop the agent. The workspace and its branch stay.
Say something to the agent.
post.description:
A message rather than keystrokes, which is the difference that matters: it
cannot arrive while the agent is not listening, and it cannot be half-typed.

get.summary: What is in this workspace that isn't safely elsewhere.

204.description: Onboarding will not be offered again

get.summary: The public half of Firetower's own ssh key.
get.description:
Read before adding a server, because the machine has to be given this before
it will let Firetower in — and that is a step on the *other* machine, which
nothing here can do.

There is no companion endpoint for the private half, and there should never
be one. It goes from the vault to a file ssh reads and no further.

AccessEntry.description: One line of the access log.

reason.description: What the credential was wanted for, in words.

Agent.description:
Which agent runs inside a workspace.

Serialised as the variant name — see the wire conventions in the brief: a
field takes the consumer's casing, an enum value stays the symbol it is.

AgentMode.description: How an agent proves who it is.

account.description: Which account this host spends against, when it will say.

checkedAt.description: When we last asked. Absent means never.

coveredByToken.description: Whether the token we hold applies to this host.

loggedIn.description:
`None` when this agent can't be asked without being started, which is
not the same as being signed out.

AgentPresence.description: What a host reported about an agent, last time we asked.

account.description:
Who it's logged in as, when it will say. Shown so you can tell which
account a host is using before it starts spending against it.

loggedIn.description: `None` when the agent offers no way to ask without starting it.

version.description: Whatever the binary printed, when it's there.

AgentView.description:
One agent kind, its configuration, and where it's actually present.

Joined here rather than left to the interface: the screen shows one row per
kind, so it should cost one request.

credentialSet.description:
Whether a credential is held. Only ever true in `ApiKey` mode — a
subscription lives in the agent's own config on the host.

oneOf.description: `None` until someone configures it.

needsCredential.description: True when nothing needs configuring, which is only the plain shell.

supported.description:
Whether Firetower can actually run this one.

An agent Firetower has no driver for is still listed — it is installed
on your hosts and you can see that it is — but a session cannot be
started on it, and a row that does not say so is a row that lets
somebody find out the hard way.

tokenCommand.description: What to run locally to get a token, when this agent works that way.

req.description: Which question. The agent's own id for the call it is blocked on.

ApiError.description: Every non-success response, so failures are as typed as everything else.

message.description:
For humans and logs. The interface should switch on `code` and write its
own copy — only it knows the context and what to offer next.

Attached.description: An image somebody put in the composer.

data.description: The bytes, base64, without a data-url prefix.

name.description: What it was called. Only the last part is kept, and it is scrubbed.

Bootstrap.description: What the web application needs before it can do anything else.

eventsPath.description:
Where the event stream lives. Config, never assumed same-origin — which
is what lets one bundle serve localhost and a hosted deployment alike.

Cause.description: What went wrong, at the granularity of what fixes it.

Checkout.description:
One repository checked out into a session's workspace.

A session used to be one of these, spread across three nullable columns on
the session itself. It is a list now, because the work is often two
repositories — a client and the API it calls — and two sessions that cannot
see each other is not an answer to that.

base.description: The branch it was cut from.

branch.description:
The branch git actually made.

Not always the one asked for: the same prompt twice wants the same
name, and git numbers the second. Per checkout because git may number
differently in each repository.

path.description:
Where it sits inside the workspace.

Empty means the checkout *is* the workspace — how every session made
before a session could hold more than one is laid out on disk. Those
directories are not moving.

pullRequest.description:
Where this repository's pull request went, once it has one.

Per repository, because that is what a git host can represent: one
change across two repositories is two pull requests that point at each
other, not one object spanning both.

oneOf.description:
Absent when the repository has since been disconnected. The slug is what
this checkout *is*, and that does not stop being true.

trouble.description:
Why it is not there, when it is not.

A repository the host could not reach fails its own checkout rather than
the session: two of three is still a session worth having, and saying
which one is missing beats pretending it was never asked for.

path.description: Relative to the workspace. Empty means the checkout is the workspace.

CheckoutSummary.description:
One checkout's summary, and which checkout it is.

A session holds any number of them, so a summary on its own no longer says
what it is a summary *of*.

CheckoutWork.description:
A checkout, what is unsaved in it, and where its pull request went.

What the interface reads to say the next honest thing — per repository, and
aggregated across them for the one button in the header.

commits.description:
Commits on this branch that its base does not have. See
[`WorkSummary::commits`]; `None` means the worker did not say.

pullRequest.description: Where its pull request is, once it has one.

trouble.description: Why this repository is not checked out, when it is not.

ClientId.description: The client id for a git host, supplied by whoever is setting this up.

clientId.description:
GitHub's looks like `Ov23li…`. Public by design: a device-flow
application has no paired secret.

message.description: The commit message. Falls back to what the agent proposed.

paths.description: Which files to include. Empty means everything that changed.

oneOf.description:
A worker as a child process here. Inherits your environment, and its
workspaces are directories you can open.

A worker in a container here. Linux, and isolated from your machine.

Reached with `docker exec` rather than ssh: the same bidirectional pipe
without an sshd, a key, or a host key to verify.

A worker on another machine. What a real deployment looks like.

Held as the parts of an ssh destination rather than one string, because
each part is a separate decision: the address is the machine, the user is
the account work runs as, and the key is which of several you keep.
Assembling them is [`Compute::ssh_destination`]'s job.

container.description:
The container the worker runs in on that machine. Absent runs the
binary on the host itself, for a machine whose image already has it.

Reached by ssh-ing to the machine and running `docker exec` there,
never by ssh-ing into the container — that would need a key inside
the image, a published port, and a host key that changes on every
recreate.

host.description: A hostname, an address, or a name from your ssh config.

hostKey.description:
Recorded when the host is added. Not yet checked against what the
machine answers with — connecting trusts a key it hasn't seen before
and remembers it, so this is a record rather than a guarantee.

key.description: Which key to authenticate with. See [`SshKey`].

port.description: Absent is whatever ssh would use: 22, or what the config says.

user.description:
Who to connect as.

Absent leaves it to ssh, which is what keeps a name from your ssh
config working on its own — that file may already say, and repeating
it here badly is worse than not repeating it.

secret.description:
The token from `claude setup-token`, or a metered API key — whichever
the mode calls for. Required for both; ignored for an agent that needs
no credential.

lastLine.description: How far this reply got. Hand it back as `sinceLine` to continue.

ConversationEvent.description:
One thing that happened, and where in the log it was said.

The line number travels with the event because several events can come from
one line, and a client's cursor has to be a position in the agent's log
rather than a count of what it drew.

oneOf.description: Allow, and stop asking about calls like this one.

reason.description:
Shown to the agent, which reads it and often tries something else.
That is the point of asking for one.

oneOf.description:
The answers to a question the agent asked.

Not an allow with extra: a question is answered, not permitted, and
letting it through without the answers gives the agent a tool result
saying nothing. Keyed by the question's own text, valued by the label
of the option chosen — the agent matches on both, so neither may be
paraphrased on the way back.

Decision.description: What the person decided, when they were asked.

Diagnosis.description:
Why a connection didn't happen, in terms of what to do about it.

Each cause has a different fix, and the failure they arrive as — a closed
stream — distinguishes none of them.

detail.description:
What the far end actually said, verbatim.

Kept even when the cause is recognised: the summary is an inference
about another machine, and this is what survives it being wrong.

remedy.description:
What to run, when there is something to run. Shown with a copy button,
so it must be the whole command and nothing else.

summary.description: One sentence, written for whoever is looking at the screen.

unreachable.description: Left alone because their host wasn't answering.

ErrorCode.description: The catalogue is the type, so there is no separate list to keep in sync.

Event.description:
Something that happened, recorded by the worker that it happened on.

Sessions are a projection of these, never the other way round.

seq.description: Monotonic per worker. This is the resume cursor.

oneOf.description:
A step is under way. Every other event here is a *completion*, which is
why a session that spent eight minutes fetching a repository looked
frozen: nothing had happened yet, so nothing had been said.

How a step is getting on, while it is still going. Sent sparingly — one
line replacing the last, not a log.

askedFor.description:
The name asked for, when it is not the name granted.

Two sessions started from the same prompt want the same branch, so
the second is numbered. That is worth saying: the branch is what a
pull request is opened from, and finding out it was renamed by
reading the pull request is finding out too late.

Renamed explicitly: this enum carries no `rename_all`, and every
other field in it happens to be one word, so it is the first that
would otherwise have reached the API as snake_case.

repo.description:
Which repository, when a session has more than one.

Absent from a worker that predates a session holding more than one,
and from a session that holds exactly one — in both cases there is
nothing to disambiguate.

note.description:
Why, when whatever changed it knows.

The agent's own words: the permission it is asking for, the last
thing it said before finishing, the error that stopped it. Without
this a blocked session is a red dot you have to open a terminal to
understand, which is most of the cost of being interrupted.

FileDiff.description: One file's worth of a unified diff.

patch.description: The hunks, as git printed them.

FileEntry.description:
One thing in a workspace directory.

Enough to draw a row and decide what to do with it, and nothing about where
it is: paths are the caller's, resolved against the workspace on the machine
that holds it.

link.description:
Shown, never followed. A repository can contain a link to `/`, and a
listing that followed one would be a file browser for the whole machine.

size.description: Zero for a directory — counting what is inside would mean walking it.

GitIdentity.description: What a person's commits are signed with, and where that came from.

source.description:
`host` — read from your token. `set` — you typed it, and nothing
overwrites it.

HeldSecret.description: A credential Firetower holds. Its name, and nothing else.

mine.description:
Yours rather than the install's. What the screen says, so it never has
to show an account id.

Host.description: A machine that can run workspaces.

oneOf.description: Why it isn't answering, when it isn't. Cleared as soon as it does.

drained.description:
Finishing what it has, taking nothing new. Separate from being
unreachable: a draining host is still online and still working.

name.description: What the user calls it. `localhost` is a real host, not a special case.

reconnecting.description:
Whether we are still trying to reach it.

A fact about the running control plane rather than about the host, so it
is answered per request and never stored. Distinguishes a machine on its
way back from one nobody is looking for.

ItemId.description: One thing in the transcript — a message, a thought, a tool call.

ItemKind.description:
What kind of thing an item is, which is what decides how it is drawn.

The list is short on purpose. It is not a catalogue of every tool an agent
might have — that changes weekly and is not knowable — but of the shapes
Firetower can draw usefully. Anything that doesn't fit is [`Unknown`], which
still renders: name, input, output. A wrong guess costs a nicer card, never
the event itself.

[`Unknown`]: ItemKind::Unknown

ItemStatus.description: How an item ended, when it has.

Me.description: Who the caller is, and what they belong to.

oneOf.description: Absent until setting up has finished.

ModelUsage.description: One model's share of a turn.

model.description:
The canonical name where the agent gives one, so `claude-opus-5[1m]`
and `claude-opus-5` are not two rows.

NewCheckout.description: One repository to check out, as the API accepts it.

base.description: The branch to start from. Omit for the repository's own default.

NewEnv.description:
Variables to hold for this repository.

Either typed one at a time, or pasted as a whole `.env` — the same route,
because they are the same thing arriving in two shapes, and the file is the
shape people already have.

dotenv.description:
A pasted `.env`, parsed here rather than in a browser: quoting is where
this goes wrong, and there should be one implementation of it.

name.description: What you'll call it. Defaults to something derived from the kind.

current.description:
The one in use. Required even when it came from a file: knowing the
session token should not be enough to lock the owner out.

body.description: Falls back to what the agent proposed, then to the session's prompt.

title.description: Written by whoever opens it, or what the agent proposed.

NewRepo.description:
Connect a repository. Nothing is cloned until a session needs it.

No default branch here on purpose. Connecting reaches for the remote anyway,
and what it answers with is the truth — a branch named by the caller was
accepted and then ignored, which is worse than not asking.

remote.description: Anything git can clone: a URL, or a path for a local repository.

setup.description: Runs once per session, before the agent starts.

NewSession.description: What the API accepts to launch one.

base.description: The branch to start from. Omit for the repository's default.

branch.description:
The branch the agent works on. Omit to derive one from the prompt.

Named by whoever starts the session, because this is what ends up on a
pull request and a machine-written slug is a poor thing to live with.

oneOf.description: Omit to let the scheduler choose.

Omit for a bare agent: a workspace with nothing checked out.

Kept alongside `repos` so that anything holding one repository still
works; when both are given, this one goes first.

repos.description:
Every repository to check out, in the order they should appear.

Each may name its own base branch; the working branch is the session's
and is the same in all of them, which is what makes a change across two
repositories reviewable.

PendingAuth.description: A device authorization waiting for someone to approve it in a browser.

userCode.description: The short code to type. Shown, not clicked.

path.description:
Where it landed, relative to the workspace — which is what to say to the
agent, and what it can act on.

PlanStep.description: One line of the agent's plan.

remote.description: A URL or a path on the host that will do the cloning.

ProbeResponse.description: What we learned by actually reaching for the repository.

defaultBranch.description: Read from the remote rather than assumed.

onlyHere.description: True when only this machine could clone it — an ssh remote or a path.

slug.description: Derived from the remote, and editable before saving.

ProviderStatus.description: What the interface shows on the connect screen.

configured.description:
False when nobody has registered an application for this build, which is
a setup problem rather than something the person using it did wrong.

connected.description: We hold a token for it.

oneOf.description: Set while an authorization is in flight.

PublicIdentity.description:
What a person may see.

The private half is not here and is not returned by anything: it goes from
the vault to a file ssh reads, and back out of existence. Every field below
is safe on a screen, in a screenshot, and in a provider's web form.

fingerprint.description:
`SHA256:…`, to match against `ssh-keygen -lf` on the other machine when
the two disagree about what was installed.

publicKey.description: `ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3… firetower`, exactly as `authorized_keys` wants it.

Question.description: Something the agent wants to know before it carries on.

header.description: A few words, for the top of the card.

question.description:
The answer is keyed by this text, so it has to survive the round trip
unchanged.

QuestionOption.description: One choice offered by a question.

label.description: What the agent expects back. Answers are keyed by this, not by position.

RawSource.description:
Which agent's output a raw frame came from.

Carried so that a frame kept for later is still interpretable later: the
bytes alone do not say whose they are.

Reached.description: What a machine would say, before anything is written down.

oneOf.description: Why not, or what is still wrong once we were in.

reached.description:
Whether ssh got onto the machine.

Not the same as "everything is fine". A machine with no worker on it has
been reached — the address, the account and the key are all right — and
is worth adding, because what is left is a command to run over there.

RemoteRepo.description: A repository the authorized account can see.

pushedAt.description: Most recently pushed first is the order people actually want.

remote.description: The https URL, since a token authenticates over https.

value.description: What to store from now on. The previous value is not recoverable.

Repo.description: A repository Firetower can cut worktrees from.

defaultBranch.description:
The trunk, once something has read the remote.

Absent until then: a repository can be connected while no worker is
reachable, and the first session to clone it fills this in.

env.description:
The names of the variables held for it, never the values.

Derived per request from the vault rather than stored, so that a screen
can say what a session will bring without opening anything.

envFile.description:
Where to write this repository's variables in the workspace.

Absent for most: the environment is enough for anything that reads
`process.env`. Present — usually `.env` — for tooling that only reads
files, and then it is written before setup runs and excluded from git.

setup.description: Runs once per session before the agent starts.

RepoChanges.description:
Change what a repository does before an agent starts.

Both fields are optional, and absent means "leave it alone" rather than
"clear it" — a form that edits one must not wipe the other.

envFile.description:
Where to write the variables in the workspace, or an empty string for
no file at all.

setup.description: A shell command, or an empty string to run nothing.

RequestId.description: One thing the agent is blocked on and needs an answer to.

RequestKind.description:
What an agent is asking permission for.

Coarser than the tool that triggered it, because the question a person is
being asked is "may this run", not "which of forty tools is this".

RevealedSecret.description: A value, on its way to a person who asked for it.

Rotated.description: What the browser that changed a password gets back.

token.description:
A new session, because the old one went with every other. Store this
and carry on — being signed out is not part of changing a password.

Session.description: A line of work with a conversation attached and a branch at the end.

branch.description:
The first checkout's branch, or `None` for a bare agent.

Every checkout in a session is cut with the same requested name, so this
is the right thing to show once — but git may have numbered them
differently, so anything acting on a branch reads it from the checkout.

checkouts.description:
Every repository checked out into this session's workspace.

Empty for a bare agent. One for most sessions. The whole point of the
list is the third case.

forgottenAt.description:
When it was removed from here without the machine being told.

Set only by a forced removal: the host was not answering, so nobody
could tear the workspace down. The session is `Ended` here from that
moment, and the agent may well still be running there.

name.description:
What to call it. `Agent 3` until somebody says otherwise.

Separate from `title`, which is cut from the prompt and describes the
work. This one identifies the session, which is a different job: five
sessions on one repository all called "Ask me…" are impossible to tell
apart, and renaming one of them to "the flaky test" fixes that.

note.description:
Why it is in that status, when whatever set it knew.

Only ever the agent's own words, and only for the statuses that mean
your move. Cleared when it goes back to working — a question that has
been answered is not worth keeping on screen.

number.description:
Assigned once, never reused, and the same for as long as the session
exists. What `name` is derived from, and what a name that has been
changed can always be traced back to.

owner.description:
Whoever started it.

Everything else about who may do what follows from this: who can open
the session, whose token pushes its branch, whose name goes on its
commits. Carried on the session rather than looked up each time,
because every one of those questions is asked while it is already
loaded.

proposedTitle.description:
What the agent proposed calling this work, when it finished.

A draft to edit rather than a box to fill. Nothing acts on it: it is
what the review sheet starts with, and whoever is shipping decides what
it actually says.

pullRequest.description:
Where the pull request is, once one has been opened.

Remembered so a screen can tell "pushed" from "already open" without
asking GitHub, which is what lets one control name the next step rather
than offering every verb at once.

repo.description:
The first checkout's slug, or `None` for a bare agent.

A convenience for the places that want one name — a row in a list, a
caption. [`Session::checkouts`] is what is actually true.

steps.description:
What this session is going to do, in order, decided when it was created.

Here rather than inferred from events so the screen has something to
show before the worker has said a word — the difference between "this
is fetching a repository" and a blank page.

title.description: Short, derived from the prompt — the prompt itself lives in the transcript.

SessionId.description: Identifies a session — the unit of work you talk to.

SetIdentity.description: What to sign commits with, typed rather than derived.

SetupState.description:
Which parts of setting up are still outstanding.

Read before anything else, so the interface knows whether to show the
wizard, and how much of it.

completed.description:
Somebody has been through onboarding, however much they skipped.

Once true it stays true: the steps after the organisation exist to point
somewhere, and a tour that reappears every time this page is opened is a
tour nobody finishes twice. Connecting GitHub later is asked for on the
screen that needs it, where there is no skipping it.

needsGithub.description:
No GitHub application is configured. Not a blocker — it is skippable,
and pasting a repository URL works without one.

needsOrganization.description: Nobody has named the organisation yet.

needsPassword.description: The signed-in account's password came from a file.

SignIn.description: What a sign-in needs from the caller.

hostId.description:
Which host should do it. Any that has the agent, by default.

It matters only in that OpenAI delivers the credential to whichever
machine asked for the code — and that machine hands it straight to us,
so which one it was stops mattering the moment it lands.

SignedIn.description: What a browser gets for a correct password.

token.description: Sent back on every later request. Said once — only its hash is kept.

SlashCommand.description: A slash command this session offers, as the agent reported it at startup.

oneOf.description:
Let ssh choose: the agent first, then the usual names in `~/.ssh`.

The default, and what an absent `identity_file` used to mean. Still
useful for a control plane running on a machine whose ssh is already
configured — a development install, or a binary on a host.

The key Firetower made for itself, sealed in the vault.

What a server added through the interface uses. Firetower holds this one
because in a container there is no other way for it to hold anything:
it is scoped to this installation, opens nothing else, and is revoked by
deleting one line on one machine.

A private key the operator pasted, sealed in the vault under this name.

For an existing key they would rather reuse, or one signed by a CA.

A path on the machine running the control plane.

Still correct when that machine is not a container. Kept so that every
host added before this existed keeps working and means what it did.

SshKey.description:
Where an agent can run.

Three kinds, and they are not a ladder — each is the right answer sometimes.
Poking at a repository by hand wants the first; leaving an agent running for
an hour wants the third.
Which private key ssh should offer when reaching a server.

This used to be one field, `identity_file`: a path on the machine running the
control plane. That was right while the control plane ran on the operator's
own machine, and stopped being right in a container — the path is read
inside the container, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` names a file that exists on their
machine and not in this one, and no path they can type would bridge the two.

So a host now says *which* key rather than *where* it is, and only one of
these is still a path.

Step.description:
One stage of bringing a session up.

The point of naming them is that the whole list is knowable *before* any of
it runs — so a session can show what it is going to do the moment it is
created, rather than assembling a shape out of events as they arrive. A step
nobody has reached yet is still worth showing.

StoredEnv.description: What was stored, and what was not.

names.description: Every variable this repository now has, in order.

skipped.description:
Lines that were skipped, and why — said rather than swallowed, because
a variable that silently never arrives is a long afternoon.

StreamKind.description:
Which stream a piece of text belongs to.

Separate from [`ItemKind`] because one item can carry more than one: a
command has both its own text and its output.

TaskId.description: One subagent run, from the moment it was spawned to its report.

images.description:
Pictures pasted or dropped into the composer.

Carried inside the message rather than written to the workspace: there
is nothing to clean up afterwards and no approval prompt for reading a
file somebody just handed over.

oneOf.description: What this session can do, reported once when the agent starts.

mode.description:
What the agent may do without asking, as it reported it.

Read rather than remembered: it is restated at the start of every
turn, so a control showing it is showing what is in force rather
than what was last requested.

oneOf.description:
Set when a subagent owns this item rather than the main thread.

Without it a subagent's tool calls interleave into the transcript
and read as though the main agent made them.

title.description: What the card is called before there is anything in it.

oneOf.description:
Something about an open item changed — usually a tool's arguments
arriving, which come a fragment at a time and are only worth showing
once they parse.
The agent is blocked and cannot continue without an answer.

args.description: The tool's full input, for a card that wants to show more.

detail.description: The command, the path — whatever a person needs to decide.

oneOf.description:
What the account's own limits say.

Arrives on its own schedule rather than with a turn, and says less than
it looks like it should: there is a window, whether we are inside it,
and when it starts again. No proportion — the agent does not send one,
and a bar drawn without one would be invented.

item.description:
The tool call that spawned it, which is how its items find their way
home.

oneOf.description:
A line we kept but could not name.

Only for what nothing else matched — the complete raw log is already
what Firetower stores, so repeating every mapped line here would double
the volume to say nothing new. This is the marker for "an agent said
something in a shape we have never seen", which is how a version that
grew a new message type shows up as a gap to fill rather than as
silence.

TurnEvent.description:
Something an agent said or did.

The vocabulary the interface draws, and the only thing that crosses out of
the normaliser.

TurnId.description: One exchange: a prompt in, and everything that happened before the agent stopped.

Usage.description:
What a turn cost, and how much room is left.

Not `Eq`, because the cost is a float. Comparing two of these for equality
is a test convenience, not something to build on.

cacheReadTokens.description: Absent when the agent does not say.

cacheWriteTokens.description:
What was written into the cache on this turn, and billed as such.

Reported apart from what was read because they cost different amounts
and mean different things: reading is the session being cheap, writing
is it having said something new and large.

contextUsed.description:
Everything the model had in front of it on the last request.

Input plus both kinds of cache plus what it wrote. This is the number
that matters to somebody deciding whether a session has room left —
input alone reads as almost nothing once caching is working, which is
exactly when it is least true.

contextWindow.description: How much room the model has at all.

costUsd.description: The agent's own estimate, in dollars. Its arithmetic, not ours.

denied.description: Tools the person refused during the turn.

durationMs.description: How long the turn took, wall clock.

firstTokenMs.description: How long before it said anything.

models.description:
What each model did, when more than one was involved.

A turn is rarely one model: something small names things and summarises
alongside the one doing the work, and it is on the bill. Totals hide
that; this does not.

thinkingTokens.description: Of the output, how much was reasoning rather than answer.

mustChangePassword.description:
True while the password came from a file rather than from a person.
Nothing but replacing it is permitted until this clears.

UserId.description: Identifies someone who can sign in.

brokenAt.description: The first entry that doesn't follow from the one before it, if any.

intact.description: Whether the log's chain of digests still holds end to end.

rootKey.description: Where the key that unlocks all of this lives — in words, never the key.

WorkSummary.description:
What is in a workspace that isn't safely elsewhere yet.

The thing that makes ending a session a decision rather than a gamble.

commits.description:
Commits on this branch that its base does not have.

Not the same question as `ahead`, which switches to measuring against
the upstream the moment a branch is pushed — so a pushed branch holding
nothing reports `ahead: 0` and looks ready to open a pull request from.
This is what says there is something to open one *for*.

`None` from a worker too old to answer, which is not the same as zero
and must not be drawn as it.

pushed.description: Whether this branch exists on the remote at all.

WorkspaceId.description: Identifies a workspace — the compute a session runs on.
